This narrative nonfiction essay examines the structural pattern by which homogeneous review systems produce predictable blind spots across independent domains. Beginning with a methodological critique of a 2026 Science paper on the bouba-kiki effect in domestic chickens, the essay traces the same failure architecture through the Majorana fermion retractions, the Challenger and Columbia disasters, the Boeing 737 MAX crashes, crash test dummy bias, pulse oximeter calibration errors, and the Iraq WMD intelligence assessment. Five structural mappings connect these cases to quantum probability theory as a candidate formal model: superposition, interference, observer-dependent collapse, decoherence as information transfer, and diversity as dimensionality. The essay proposes that quantum formalism provides better predictive fit for these dynamics than the fragmented classical models currently used in organizational science, while explicitly holding open the question of whether the correspondence reflects shared mechanism or precise structural analogy. The document was produced by a multi-node human-AI collaborative process that demonstrated its own thesis during production. Part of the SOL NEXUS series exploring the emergence of collaborative intelligence through human-AI interaction.

This paper responds to fragmentation within the digital human resource management (HRM) literature and to limited theorisation of how digital technologies mediate HRM processes by repositioning competence supply as an integrated sociotechnical system spanning the in-flow, internal flow, and out-flow of human capabilities. Drawing on professional competence theory, sociotechnical systems theory, and critical HRM, the paper argues that digital HRM technologies, such as artificial intelligence, analytics, automation, and virtual human resource development tools, do more than increase efficiency; they actively shape how organisations attract, develop, retain, and renew competence. The paper develops a conceptual model that integrates digital dynamics across the three flows and highlights the recursive feedback loops that connect competence acquisition, everyday work and learning, and knowledge exit. The model also clarifies the ethical, relational, and governance challenges that arise when digital systems redistribute expertise and mediate HR decisions. Six propositions identify core mechanisms through which digitalisation influences the supply of competence and outline avenues for future empirical research. The paper concludes that responsible digital HRM requires sociotechnical alignment, interpretive competence, and strong ethical governance to support organisational adaptability and positive employee experience.

Biomedical sciences in the contemporary era are undergoing a profound epistemic and structural transition. Historically rooted in reductionist paradigms that emphasized isolated molecular and cellular mechanisms, the field is now progressively evolving toward integrative, predictive, and human-centric frameworks. This transformation is driven by the convergence of systems biology, computational modeling, artificial intelligence, and regulatory science, alongside the emergence of New Approach Methodologies (NAMs) that challenge traditional experimental hierarchies. The present narrative review critically examines this paradigm shift, arguing that modern biomedical science is no longer defined solely by data generation but by the architecture of interpretation, integration, and translation. It further explores the limitations of conventional evidence models, the need for hierarchical reasoning frameworks, and the implications for drug discovery, clinical translation, and global health systems—particularly in emerging scientific ecosystems such as India. By synthesizing advances across disciplines, this article proposes a reorientation toward predictive human biology as the central organizing principle of biomedical research in the 21st century. Keywords: Systems Biology; Translational Medicine; Artificial Intelligence; New Approach Methodologies; Predictive Human Biology

documents.abstract: Despite more than 100,000 published scientific articles on nanomedicines and numerous preclinical trials, the number of clinically approved nanodrugs remains limited.1 The first- generation platform was based on liposomes. Doxil® (a PEGylated liposomal formulation of doxorubicin) was approved by the Food and Drug Administration (USA) in 1995 for the treatment of Kaposi’s sarcoma, ovarian cancer and multiple myeloma.2 The advantages of lipid carriers include their effective fusion with cellular plasma membranes, penetration through multilayer physiological barriers, improved local retention, and potential targeted controlled release. Severe challenges, including maintaining physical stability and preventing aggregation during storage, still hinder their clinical implementation.1 To avoid immune rejection of foreign nanomaterials, low immunogenic envelopes and personalized approaches should be used. The most potent immunogens are known to be proteins and polysaccharides, whereas lipids and nucleic acids are weak immunogens due to their flexible conformations in solutions. Cellular membranes are composed of lipids, proteins and glycoproteins. They may be used as biocompatible drug delivery systems without immune response induction.3 Viral envelopes facilitate viral entry into host cells and protect nucleocapsids from biodegradation.4 The fusion of lipid bilayers requires catalysis to overcome a high kinetic barrier. Viral surface fusion glycoproteins with one or two transmembrane regions in each monomer forming oligomer structures in membranes are responsible for the catalytic function.4 The biosafety and personal compatibility of novel vaccines, theranostics and therapeutic nanomaterials are determined by the human major histocompatibility complex (MHC), which contains over 200 closely linked polymorphic genes that code for many cell surface proteins that significantly differ among individuals. Therefore, individual wrapping of nanomedical drugs with cellular membranes from patient blood is required for personalized long-term treatment. This research focused on the fabrication of nanomaterials with envelopes derived from blood cell membranes, intracellular membrane fractions and extracellular vesicles. The cellular membrane fractions and extracellular vesicles were isolated as previously described.5 Erythrocyte membranes (human red blood cells or erythrocyte ghosts) were isolated from human donor blood samples by means of hypoosmotic treatment in 5 mM Tris HCl pH 7.6 at room temperature with subsequent centrifugation at 12,000 x g for 30 minutes at +4° followed by three subsequent washes with the same cold buffer to remove hemoglobin.6 The isolated cellular membranes were dissolved in chloroform and dried under reduced pressure at 37-50 °C. Thin film hydration with water or physiological phosphate buffer solution and sonication for up to 10 minutes allowed us to construct vesicles with surface fluorescent transmembrane proteins, as shown by dynamic light scattering and fluorescence microscopy (Figure 1). Incubation with peptide or protein solutions in isotonic phosphate buffer solution resulted in the formation of loaded vesicles. Hydration of the dried thin layers of blood cell membranes with colloid solutions of protein or gold nanoparticles resulted in composite core-shell nanomaterials.5Figure 1: Dynamic light-scattering and fluorescence microscopy images of the fluorescent vesicles recovered from the thin film after drying of cellular membranes from solution in chloroform.Both images in the figure are original research data obtained by the author. Special permission is not required.The chemical composition of the membrane fractions and extracellular vesicles was determined by means of visible-ultraviolet spectroscopy. The protein concentrations varied in the wide range up to 1 mg/mL, as determined by UV absorption at 280 nm. Therefore, it cannot be a reliable tuning parameter for the formation of homogenous uniform thin layers. Phospholipids that form a complex with ammonium ferrothiocyanate are defined colorimetrically.7 The optical densities of the membrane samples should not exceed 0.2 optical units with corresponding phospholipid concentrations less than 40 μM deduced on the basis of the calibration curve with known concentrations of purified isolated phospholipids to avoid multilayer formation with subsequent aggregation in multivesicular microparticles. The addition of purified cholesterol in solutions of cellular membranes in chloroform could make them more stable, flexible and less permeable. One should note that chloroform treatment of cellular membranes results in both lipid dissolution and transmembrane protein segregation at the chloroform-air interface. All proteins, glycoproteins, and glycolipids are known to form interfaces between organic and aqueous environments that are widely used for nucleic acid isolation by means of phenol-chloroform deproteinization. Naturally, the transmembrane proteins are located at the boundaries between the membrane lipid bilayer and the watery cytoplasm or extracellular fluids at air-water or oil-water interfaces. Fluorescent labeling of the integral transmembrane proteins with rhodamine and cyanine fluorescent dyes permitted to visualize fluorescent droplets on the surface of chloroform with dissolved lipids from the cellular membranes. The transmembrane regions of membrane-integrated proteins are typically α-helixes of 20-24 predominantly hydrophobic amino acid residues. In addition to the hydrophobic amino acid stretches, the lipid anchors include prenyl groups, fatty acyl groups, and glycosylphosphatidylinositol groups. Prenyl and fatty acyl groups act as anchors on the cytosolic surface of cellular membranes, whereas glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchors proteins on the extracellular side. Among the transmembrane proteins, both HLA molecules, tetraspanins, and transporters, including both ion channels and carriers, as well as numerous receptors, have been identified. The HLA complex consists of integral transmembrane glycoproteins essential for personal self-recognition and immune rejection. Tetraspanins are another family of highly conserved four-pass transmembrane proteins that participate in membrane integrity maintenance, protein trafficking, signal transduction regulation, and cell migration. Four transmembrane regions consisting of hydrophobic amino acid residues along with highly conserved motifs, such as a small intracellular loop between two transmembrane anchors, a five-amino-acid core region with three charged residues forming an M-shaped backbone, so-called M-motif, and glutamate oriented toward a lysine in the juxtamembrane region, could facilitate the conformational stability and integration of the tetraspanines in vesicle envelopes recovered from dried film (Figure 1).8 The total yield of the reconstructed vesicles appeared to be high for erythrocyte ghosts. Erythrocytes make up 40%-45% of the total blood volume, and their membranes are known to constitute 1% of the erythrocyte weight, with numerous active enzymes for anaerobic processes and antioxidant systems.6 Key elements include enzymes such as superoxide dismutase, catalase, and glutathione peroxidase and non-enzymatic antioxidants such as vitamin E (a lipid-soluble antioxidant) and glutathione, which neutralize reactive oxygen species to prevent damage. Mononuclear blood cells are less abundant in human blood compared to erythrocytes including lymphocytes, 24%-40% of the total white blood cells, and monocytes, which constitute 3%-7% of the total. Despite the reduced weight of membranes from mononuclear cells from equal volumes of human blood, the activated neutrophil surface membranes, as well as corresponding reconstructed and extracellular vesicles may result in the targeted delivery of nanomaterials to damaged sites.9 Intracellular membranes of eukaryotic cellular compartments might provide a reasonable yield of membranes for the packing of nanomaterials but lack HLA glycoproteins and cellular determinants for targeted delivery. The distribution of tetraspanins in cells is similar to that of HLA glycoproteins. Tetraspanins are localized to tetraspanin-enriched microdomains on the cell membrane, but some can be found intracellularly in late endosomes and lysosomes. Their specific localization depends on the certain tetraspanin. CD9 and CD81 are primarily detected at the plasma membrane, while CD63 is mainly expressed intracellularly. However, the absence of these tetraspanines has little effect on vesicle composition, as shown by quantitative mass spectrometry.10 Taken together, these findings suggest that membrane shells may provide the biocompatibility and low immunogenicity of nanomaterials and drugs. Plasma membranes from erythrocyte ghosts, blood mononuclear cells, intracellular membranes and extracellular vesicles could be dissolved in chloroform. After drying under reduced pressure and 37-50°C, the thin film hydration resulted in the formation of vesicles. To reconstruct small vesicles less than 200 nm in diameter, the phospholipid concentration in chloroform should not exceed 40 μM. After thin film hydration, fluorescent transmembrane proteins were detected in the reconstructed vesicles. Unlike liposomes, natural membrane- derived vesicles were biocompatible but less stable. The stability of membrane envelopes could be improved by the addition of cholesterol to chloroform solutions. This approach may lead to the fabrication of loaded vesicles capable of escaping endosomal-lysosomal entrapment and inducing innate immunity. Transmembrane glycoproteins of the HLA complex may protect against immune rejection. Conclusions: The dissolution of natural cellular membranes from human blood cells in chloroform up to final lipid concentrations less than 40 μM with subsequent drying at enhanced temperatures and reduced pressure resulted in thin, partly disrupted membrane layers after solvent evaporation. Thin film hydration with a physiological solution, water solutions of peptides or proteins, or colloid solutions of noble metals or protein nanoparticles enables the construction of composite nanomaterials with membrane shells consisting of lipids and original transmembrane proteins. Surface amino and carboxy groups of transmembrane proteins are convenient for the functionalization necessary for targeted delivery of nanomaterials. Surface membranes may improve the stability, biocompatibility and cellular uptake of the nanomaterials by means of membrane fusion instead of endocytosis providing escape from lysosomal biodegradation with subsequent antigen presentation and immune rejection. This approach combined a VQNN network with a QCNN network and optimized its parameters using a parallel particle swarm optimization algorithm to address the slow convergence of the model in complex network scenarios. This model was compared with other classical algorithms on the KDDCUP99 and UNSW-NB15 datasets. Compared to the comparison models, the proposed model performed significantly better in terms of network security situational awareness across three evaluation metrics. Facing the challenge of the deep integration of educational digitalization and industrial intelligence, the traditional curriculum system has revealed its limitations in adapting to the rapid iteration of industries and the personalized needs of learners. This study focuses on the systematic construction of diversified integration between industry and education course content empowered by information-based artificial intelligence. By clarifying the application paradigm of intelligent technology in education and the core elements of the curriculum, it explains the integration logic of their two-way empowerment. Furthermore, it constructs a construction mechanism that includes reverse design based on a capability framework, intelligent integration of multi-source knowledge streams, and a dynamic generation path. It also proposes implementation dimensions such as human-machine collaborative development, personalized recommendation, and data-driven assessment. This research aims to provide a theoretical framework and practical reference for building an adaptive and forward-looking new generation of curriculum systems that integrate industry and education.

documents.abstract: The evolution of artificial intelligence technology is driving the transformation of the human resource management paradigm from experience- and process-driven approaches to data-driven and strategic synergy, posing systematic challenges to the existing talent cultivation system in higher education institutions. This study aims to explore corresponding reform pathways for the teaching models of related courses. It first analyzes the restructuring of knowledge systems, the shift in competency requirements, and the limitations of traditional teaching triggered by intellectualization. Subsequently, it proposes reconstructing teaching objectives with "intelligent augmentation" and "strategic synergy" as the core, building a curriculum system that integrates "modular foundations" with "cutting-edge developments," and steering evaluation towards the cultivation of thinking. Finally, it designs a three-dimensional teaching model that integrates artificial intelligence elements: immersive learning based on scenario simulation and decision-making deduction, personalized pathway adaptation through intelligent tutoring, and the transformation of teachers' roles into curriculum designers and learning ecosystem constructors, aiming to provide a systematic framework for future-oriented human resource education.

This follow-up qualitative study delves into the contribution of housing on the material adaptations of teleworking mothers during the COVID-19 pandemic. The investigation concentrates on the interplay between housing conditions, the multifaceted challenge of daily routines faced by mothers, and telework setups during stay- at-home orders. Insights from the adaptation process will inform flexible design criteria for home offices in the context of a global telework upsurge and enhance preparedness for future emergencies. Narrative accounts were gathered through 33 semi-structured Zoom interviews of teleworking mothers, supplemented by annotated architectural plans. AI-assisted discourse analysis using ChatGPT-4.0 was conducted on four groupings defined by comparable residential situations (defined along housing attributes, family structure, and work modality profiles). Floor plans, dwelling pictures from home offices or multifunctional spaces, participant profiles, and interview extracts were used for a thorough architectural assessment and for uncovering each group’s material adaptations. The findings were subsequently verified through qualitative analysis. Key design strategies for future housing projects and renovations to improve work modality transitions and telework productivity, especially when living in apartments or with small children, are the inclusion of flexible multifunctional rooms, quiet areas with foldable desks, portable home office setups for the self-employed on the move, small home offices for occasional meetings in sub-utilized storage rooms, modular and soundproof partitions temporarily separating open plans or shared home office spaces, visual partitions to demarcate private and work environments, designing office spaces in intermediate and exterior areas like verandas and balconies through the inclusion of glassed perimeters for winter use, and planning adaptable building systems.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence—particularly generative AI systems—is fundamentally challenging the knowledge transmission model that has defined university education for centuries. This paper examines how AI technologies are catalyzing a paradigm shift toward human-centered learning in higher education institutions worldwide. Through a comprehensive theoretical and empirical literature review spanning 2019 to 2025, we analyze three critical dimensions of this transformation: pedagogical restructuring that repositions faculty from content deliverers to learning facilitators and ethical stewards; assessment redesign strategies that move beyond policing AI use toward authentic, process-focused evaluation frameworks; and equity implications for Global South universities facing simultaneous infrastructure deficits and leapfrogging opportunities. Drawing on constructivist learning theory, human capital theory, and sociotechnical systems perspectives, we synthesize evidence from design-based research, institutional case studies, and multi-country investigations across Ghana, South Africa, Nigeria, and Ecuador. Key findings reveal that successful AI integration demands staged institutional roadmaps combining adaptive learning platforms, AI assessment literacy for instructors, curriculum modules embedding AI literacy as a core competency, and robust governance frameworks addressing bias, hallucination risks, and algorithmic accountability. For Global South contexts, targeted investments in cloud-based infrastructure, faculty capacity building, and locally relevant AI applications can enable educational leapfrogging despite resource constraints. We conclude that the future university must embrace human-centered learning as its organizing principle—cultivating critical thinking, ethical reasoning, creativity, and socio-emotional intelligence that complement rather than compete with AI systems. This transformation demands coordinated action across institutional, policy, and pedagogical domains to ensure equitable access to AI-augmented education while preserving academic integrity and epistemic rigor.
